interest: This file is exceptionally valuable for historians of the Allied Occupation of Japan, modern labor history, and post-war legal reform, as it provides the primary English texts of the foundational legislative architecture that re-established and legalized independent trade unionism in Japan. Transmitted by GHQ/SCAP's Economic and Scientific Section, it reflects the early implementation of General MacArthur's October 1945 democratization directive mandating the emancipation of Japanese workers and the encouragement of unionization. The documents demonstrate how the conservative Shidehara cabinet adapted Anglo-American collective bargaining concepts—including unfair labor practice protections, immunity from criminal prosecution and civil damage claims for legitimate dispute acts, and tripartite Labor Relations Committees—while simultaneously embedding significant administrative supervision by prefectural governors and maintaining state prohibitions against union membership for police, firefighters, and penal staff. The legislative enactments also capture cabinet transitions during early 1946, evidenced by the change in the Minister of Transportation countersignature from Takeo Tanaka in December 1945 to Yoshishige Murakami in February 1946.
overview: This file contains an official English-language legal compilation entitled 'Basic Japanese Labor Union Legislation,' prepared in March 1946 by the Economic and Scientific Section of the General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (GHQ/SCAP) and transmitted as an enclosure to Despatch No. 365 from Tokyo to the U.S. Department of State. The document reproduces official English translations presented by the Imperial Japanese Government of three cornerstone post-World War II labor measures: the Trade Union Law (promulgated on December 21, 1945), Imperial Ordinance No. 107 (promulgated on February 27, 1946, establishing March 1, 1946, as the enforcement date), and Imperial Ordinance No. 108 (the Enforcement Ordinance of the Trade Union Law, promulgated on February 27, 1946). Together, these legislative instruments dismantled pre-war authoritarian restrictions, established workers' fundamental rights to organize, bargain collectively, and strike with immunity from criminal sanctions and employer damage claims, regulated the legal personality and registration of unions, instituted compulsory extension of collective agreements, and established tripartite Labor Relations Committees (Central, Prefectural, and Special) to mediate and arbitrate industrial disputes across occupied Japan.

subfiles.about: The Trade Union Law legalizes labor unions in Japan, guarantees the rights of workers to organize and bargain collectively, and establishes tripartite Labor Relations Committees.
subfiles.summary: Promulgated on December 21, 1945, by Emperor Hirohito following approval by the Imperial Diet, this foundational statute establishes legal protections for Japanese workers and labor organizations. It guarantees the rights to organize, conduct collective bargaining, and engage in strikes and dispute acts with immunity from criminal charges under Article 35 of the Criminal Code and employer damage claims. The law prohibits unfair labor practices such as dismissal or discrimination for union membership, provides for the legal enforceability and regional extension of collective agreements, and establishes tripartite Labor Relations Committees at national and prefectural levels to mediate and arbitrate disputes. Police, firemen, and penal institution personnel are excluded from the right to organize, while public employees are subject to separate regulations.
subfiles.title: Trade Union Law, promulgated 21 December 1945

subfiles.about: Imperial Ordinance No. 107 fixes March 1, 1946, as the official date of enforcement for the Trade Union Law.
subfiles.summary: Sanctioned on February 26, 1946, and promulgated on February 27, 1946, by Emperor Hirohito with the countersignatures of Prime Minister Kijuro Shidehara and key cabinet ministers, this imperial ordinance consists of a single operative article. It decrees that the Trade Union Law approved by the Imperial Diet on December 21, 1945, shall come into force effective March 1, 1946. The ordinance was issued pursuant to the supplementary regulations of the Trade Union Law requiring that its enforcement date be determined by Imperial Ordinance.
subfiles.title: Ordinance Fixing Date of Enforcement of the Trade Union Law (Imperial Ordinance No. 107)

subfiles.about: Imperial Ordinance No. 108 sets forth detailed administrative regulations, registration procedures, court dissolution rules, and operational guidelines for Labor Relations Committees under the Trade Union Law.
subfiles.summary: Promulgated on February 27, 1946, this extensive 48-article imperial ordinance provides the procedural apparatus necessary to implement the Trade Union Law upon its entry into force on March 1, 1946. It designates prefectural governors and the Welfare Minister as competent administrative authorities, establishes detailed requirements for trade union registration and legal personality at local district courts, and regulates judicial proceedings for union dissolution under the Non-contentious Procedures Law. The ordinance also details the composition, appointment, and operations of the Central, Prefectural, and Special Labor Relations Committees, requiring equal tripartite representation of employers, workers, and neutral members with one-year terms. Special administrative provisions are established for maritime labor under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Transportation and the Maritime Transportation Bureau.
subfiles.title: Enforcement Ordinance of the Trade Union Law (Imperial Ordinance No. 108)
